item.title: The librarian: my favourite agent, and why a data platform needs a library at its heart, a catalogue of everything PrompTugal.news has read, each item with its source, licence, evidence and links, a graph of how it all connects, an invitation to real librarians, and the next shelves, official sources and the law
item.description: The librarian has always been my favourite agent. When a team of agents reads hundreds of sources a day, someone has to know what was read, where it came from, what it may be used for, and how it connects to everything else. Today PrompTugal.news gave that job its own site: library.promptugal.news, "everything we found, catalogued, sourced and linked". It holds 78 items so far, from the summit's official replays and other people's recordings to our own coverage and seven recorded gaps, each on its own card, what it is, who made it, when and where, its source, its licence, its evidence, and how it connects to the rest; all of it as JSON anyone can use. Behind it, a librarian with a team of its own, an ontologist, a cartographer, a graph keeper, a historian and a reality check, learning from the library our SGraph Send team built as a graph. And on the site, an invitation to librarians, the people, to work with it. The next shelves are the ones I care about most: official sources, government data and the law as it stands, so that every claim about a place can be checked against them. We should be finding budget to hire librarians for this. Part five of the series.

item.title: Ten days to a data platform: how PrompTugal.news went from a newsroom at Web Summit to twelve public data sources, a register of 92 sources read and not read, a dozen sites on its own domain and two cyber-threat feeds cleared to run, with a security agent on every change, and why each step made the next one cheaper
item.description: The first commit of PrompTugal.news was at 00:08 on 4 November: a newsroom for Web Summit. Two weeks and 6,790 commits later it is a data platform for Portugal's places. The storm site went live just after midnight on 11 November. On 15 November we gave every place its own agent: Portugal, the Algarve and each of its towns, with a behaviour policy each. On 17 November, one decision about the site factory let us create a data site, and then five more sites in one request: weather, travel, civic, startups and the data itself. Today, 18 November, the team added an events site, a register of 92 sources with the reason we do or do not read each, three new data sources, a library, video and webcam sites, and a cyber-threat site whose first two feeds, the known exploited vulnerabilities and the CVE list, were cleared to run by the security agent. Every change now passes a security review before and after. This is part one of the series, the timeline, and the point of it: each step made the next one cheaper, so the speed keeps growing.

item.title: Sites on the data: what happens when a data platform meets a factory that makes a site in minutes, a page that draws IPMA's data six ways, an invented holiday-homes company whose bookings are simulated and whose weather, sea and events are real, demos for weather, events and cyber, and how each experiment, a new industry, a new view, a new idea, is now a site published in ten or twenty minutes
item.description: The data platform and the site factory meet in a way I did not plan, and it may be the most interesting part of all. Because any site can now read PrompTugal.news's public data, and the factory can make a site in under a minute, every idea becomes a site. This morning, at 10:36, I asked for a site showing the IPMA data we have; by 10:48 ipma-data.agenticcells.site was live, drawing IPMA's warnings, forecasts and readings six ways, from a broadsheet weather page to a night-desk board to a single A4 almanac. This afternoon the factory made Cinco Chaminés, an invented company with five holiday homes from Tavira to Sagres: the homes, prices and bookings are simulated and say so, but the weather, the sea, the UV and the local events for your dates are real, read live from the data platform, with links to live beach cameras. Then demos for weather, events and cyber, and a simulated London billboard. This is what I mean by intersection: a real-estate site is more useful with what to do there, the weather and the sea; and each of those is one more data source on the platform. And every experiment, a new industry, a new view, a new way to read the same data, is a demo for what an agentic cell can do. Part four of the series.

item.title: Paying the sources: the business model behind PrompTugal.news's data, a reader's money flowing back to the sources the reader actually read, worked out in the open and simulated for now, a licence link on every value, a public register of who we read and who we do not, and why a platform built on public data with no lock-in can be a positive loop for everyone who feeds it
item.description: My business model for this platform is a positive feedback loop: the reader pays for what they read, and the money flows back to the sources that made it possible, in a way the reader can see. Today the PrompTugal.news team built the first version of that, as a simulation. A page shows how a reader's £5 would be shared: 30% kept for costs, the rest split among the sources behind the pages they read, weighted by how each was used, a cited fact, quoted words, a data set, a lead; 504 sources behind 112 pages, IPMA's data at the top. No money moves yet, and every page says so. Beside it, every value the sites serve now carries a link to its licence, and a public register lists 92 sources, the 18 we read and the 74 we do not, quoting why. There is no lock-in: everything is published, built on public data, with its evidence. And the gaps are the next step: some publishers do not allow their data to be shown, even data their own users gave them, and the answer is to ask them, on the record, and to make paying them part of the offer. Part three of the series.

item.title: One commit, one site, one owner: the small change to the AgentiCCells site factory that unblocked the most, giving a GitHub account access to the repository it creates, so that one commit with a site's details and its owner's account makes the repository, the DNS record in AWS, the address, HTTPS and the owner's access in under a minute, and all that is left is to point Claude at it
item.description: Some of the things that make the biggest difference are hard to measure, and small. On 17 November, at about 18:20, I said yes to a change in the AgentiCCells site factory, "since it will really make a massive difference": a second domain, a GitHub token per owner, and collaborators. The last one is the detail. The factory could already turn a request file in a commit into a GitHub repository, a DNS record in AWS, a seeded site, its address and HTTPS. Now the same request can name the GitHub accounts that should have access, and the factory invites them at the end. So one commit with the details of a site and its owner's account does everything: when events.promptugal.news was created today, the factory validated the request at 14:28:12, created the repository four seconds later, seeded it, configured it, set the DNS record, enforced HTTPS at 14:29:06 and gave the owner's account access at 14:29:07, 55 seconds in all. The factory has now handled 36 requests. And the hand-over is one sentence: point your Claude at this repository, and start editing. Part two of the series.

item.title: Gaining speed: a series on what happens when you productise the way you build, PrompTugal.news going from a newsroom at Web Summit to a data intelligence platform for Portugal's places in two weeks, a factory that turns one commit into a site with its owner, money that flows back to the sources, sites built on the data in minutes, the librarian, and a team like this for sale
item.description: Two weeks ago PrompTugal.news was a newsroom we started for Web Summit. Today it is something else: twelve public data sources collected by code, a register of 92 sources read and not read with the reason for each, a dozen sites on its own domain, from weather and events to civic, startups and a library, a security agent checking every change, and a simulated payout that shows how a reader's money would flow back to the sources. In the last day alone the team added three data sources, cleared two cyber-threat feeds, and the factory created six new sites. That is what happens when you productise the way you build: you keep gaining speed. This series tells it in parts. First, the timeline. Then the small thing that unblocked the most: a factory that turns one commit into a repository, an address and its owner's access. Then the business model: money back to the sources, in the open. Then the sites built on top of the data, a real-estate demo with real weather and events among them, each made in minutes. Then the librarian, my favourite agent. And last, the offer: a team like this one, for sale, with the code open and the data public.

item.title: A team like this, for sale: what we sell is not the platform, it is the agentic team that built it, its roles, its behaviour policies, its security passes and its speed, with the code open and the data public, and who I want to talk to now that PrompTugal.news is a working data platform and not an experiment
item.description: The last part of the series is the offer. Everything I have described, a newsroom that became a data platform in two weeks, a factory that turns a commit into a site and its owner's access, money flowing back to the sources, sites built on the data in minutes, a library at the heart of it, was built by an agentic team: conductors, a place agent for every town, data agents, a security agent reviewing every change before and after, a behaviour policy for every agent, a librarian. That team is what we sell. The code is open source and the data is public, so anyone can take it; what a customer buys is a team like this one, set up for them, with its policies, running their sources, their sites and their workflows, at the speed they have seen here. It is a live demo of what an agentic team does under agent behaviour policies. And now that PrompTugal.news is a working platform and not a small experiment, I want to talk to the people who could use it, integrate with it, fund it or feed it: councils and regional bodies, tourism, universities, newsrooms, the platforms we cannot read yet, and anyone who needs to know what is happening in a place. Part six of the series.

item.title: A factory that films its work: a review of ESF, Mitko Vasilev's open-source Engineering Software Factory, one task into one microVM, one agent, deterministic gates and a verified patch with its evidence, the demo videos and review queue his post shows, which are not yet in the public repository, and what our own factories should take from it, starting with a recording made by the same run that proves the change
item.description: Mitko Vasilev posted that his software factory has started making video demos: it takes bugs and features from the backlog, runs them through a Temporal workflow, a coding agent in a disposable sandbox and deterministic verification gates, and he came back from a meeting to a reviewed change, the agent's full trajectory, all the traces and a 14-second clip of the feature working, recorded by the same run that proves it. I like that last idea a lot, so I read his repository, github.com/mitkox/esf. ESF, the Engineering Software Factory, is serious work: MIT-licensed, mostly Go, at version 1.0.0-rc.1, with a clear rule, "one task in, one isolated Cube microVM, one agent, one verified patch out". Each run gets its own microVM, credentials are injected at the network edge and never placed in the sandbox, the gates read exit codes so "the model never declares success", a behaviour monitor can quarantine a run, and every run leaves an evidence folder and OpenTelemetry traces. What the public repository does not have yet is the part of the post that caught my eye: no video recording, no backlog connector, no pull requests and no review queue with approve, reject and defer; the screenshot shows a separate application. That is not a criticism: the core is the hard part, and it is open. Here is what it does, how it compares with our own factories, and what we should take from it: the recording from the run that proves the change, a gate that stops a change rewriting its own gates, and a sandbox per run.

item.title: Whose event is it? Why Luma, Eventbrite, Meetup and Partiful will not let a site like PrompTugal.news show the public events their organisers want seen, what their terms actually say, who owns an event listing, what UK, EU and Portuguese law allows, what organisers expect, and how PrompTugal.news now collects events with a legal basis and the evidence for every one
item.description: Our agents found something I find strange. The platforms where most events are published, Luma, Eventbrite, Meetup and Partiful, do not let a site like PrompTugal.news include their events. If I published an event, I would want it shown as widely as possible, and a site that lists it and links back sends people to the platform, where they still register. So I asked for the analysis. What the terms say: Eventbrite forbids scraping outright; Partiful forbids scraping and copying; Luma allows access only through its supported interfaces and forbids republishing images; Meetup's API needs a paid Pro plan. Who owns the listing: the organiser, not the platform; each platform takes a non-exclusive licence, which means the organiser can give us the same right. What the law says: bare facts, the date, time, place and title, are not protected by copyright; descriptions and photographs are, and belong to the organiser or the photographer; database right and the platforms' contracts are the real constraints on copying a platform's listings wholesale; guests' names are personal data and stay out. So the distribution organisers are promised is distribution to partners the platform chooses. Our principle is that we publish only what we have a legal basis to publish, with the evidence. The routes that meet it are the organiser's own permission, official agendas we may read, and the facts with a link, as a search engine shows them; and PrompTugal.news's new events site and register of sources already work that way. One more finding: part of what blocked us was our own house rule, not the platforms' terms.

item.title: RiskMandate and Kosmoy: two answers to "who controls the agents?", Kosmoy's self-hosted control plane for regulated enterprises, with an AI gateway, guardrails, a model router, observability and a Kubernetes sandbox for every agent run, and RiskMandate's open behaviour policies, written per agent, checked by hooks and bounded by SHarness, where they overlap, where they differ, and why they fit together
item.description: I was asked how RiskMandate compares with Kosmoy, so I read Kosmoy's site properly. Kosmoy, from Milan, sells what it calls the AI management platform for regulated enterprises: an inventory of every AI use case, model, agent and MCP server; an AI gateway that is "one policy point for every AI call", with guardrails, role-based access, routing between small and frontier models, cost tracking and logging; and the Action Capsule, a Kubernetes sandbox for each agent run, with admission before it starts, run-scoped credentials, an egress allow-list and a kill switch. It runs single-tenant in the customer's own cluster, is priced by proposal, and names Banca d'Italia and Leonardo as customers. RiskMandate starts from the other end: a written behaviour policy for each agent, what it can reach, what it was authorised to do, the gap between them, and what stands in the way, published as an open standard, checked on every call by hooks, and, at the strongest, bounded by SHarness at the kernel; starting at £0, because the standard, the policies and the code are all open source, and sold from £500 for one agent to £20,000 for an estate, with every price on the page and every claim linked to our own agents' records. Kosmoy is the enforcement plant; RiskMandate is the policy and the evidence. The obvious fit: an Agent Behaviour Policy is exactly what Kosmoy's gateway and capsules could enforce.

item.title: A guide born in a storm: when Storm Charles cancelled Web Summit's second day, the whole team built Lisbon Tech Fringe, a guide to the city's side events, from a spoken brief at 10:00 to its own address by about 12:57, 179 events and 104 communities each re-read at its source, one conductor per person, terms respected source by source, a guest-list hold, every agent traced, and a graph you can query in your browser
item.description: On the morning of 11 November, with Web Summit's second day cancelled by Storm Charles, Lisbon was full of people with nowhere to go and dozens of side events nobody was mapping in one place. At about 10:00 I said we should start a site for everything else that was happening: an alternative summit, an event site. By 10:30 the brief was written and pasted into a conductor on another account, ending "Yes to all of it. Go." Within a couple of hours there was a site, and by about 12:57 it served at its own address, lisbontechfringe.com. It was built by everyone on the team at once, each person running their own conductor, with me as the head conductor. By the next evening it listed 179 events and 104 communities, each event re-read at its public source with the time it was read, labelled fact or evidence, and marked when the storm had moved it. The agents read only sources whose terms allowed it, and refused or held the rest. They held a public key for their captures of event pages, because those pages showed guests' names. Every run was traced into Elastic, the work became a graph in Neo4j, and anyone could query the whole guide in SQL in their own browser. Part nine of the series.

item.title: From a feed to meaning: what the Storm Charles site did with public data that our new data site does not do yet, finding a source, reading its terms, writing parsers, keeping provenance, drawing it and saying what it means, three source sites to show it hourly, for the weather, the sea and fire risk, and the relay of briefs from this newsroom to the agents that will build them
item.description: Comparing the Storm Charles site with our new data site, data.promptugal.news, shows the difference between collecting data and understanding it. In a night, the storm site found its sources, read their terms, wrote parsers and converters, kept every value with its source and time, labelled each line fact, evidence or hypothesis, drew it a dozen ways, the lead time from warning to decision, warned against observed, a replay, and then said what it meant. The data site, built yesterday from my brief, does the first half very well: nine public sources, IPMA's warnings, observations, forecasts, fire risk, sea and UV, MeteoAlarm and flights around Faro, collected by code, served as JSON with an API and an OpenAPI description, each value with its provenance. It does not yet draw it, explain it, or show anyone how to use it; and when I checked this morning, the "hourly" data had last been read at 02:28, six hours earlier. So here is the next step: three source sites, website cells each built on one feed that changes through the day, the weather and its warnings, the sea, and fire risk, each rebuilt every hour, each with its charts, a plain "what changed", and a page on how to use the data. It is a working example of connecting any data with any data. And the way this brief travels is itself the example: from this newsroom, to PrompTugal's conductor, to the conductor on another account, to the agent that runs the data; and to the AgentiCCells team that will build the sites.

item.title: Start with an interview: how someone goes from "I want to try it" to editing their own site with Claude, by being interviewed by Claude first, about what they want, the sections, their materials and the sites they like, then sending their material in whichever way suits them, getting five designs inspired by what they like, or a better version of the site they already have, and reaching the one milestone that matters
item.description: When someone says "cool, I want to try it", what happens next decides whether they ever get a website. Today the first step on agenticcells.ai is an email with our questions in it. I think we can do something much better, and show the power of Claude at the same time: start with an interview. Claude interviews the person about what they want the site to do, the sections they would like, the materials and documents they have, and, the question I like most, which websites they like and why. The answers become the brief. The material can come in whatever way suits them: a zip, an email, links to what is already public, or their own encrypted vault; and the interviewing Claude can even be the one that starts building. The five designs are then inspired by the sites they chose, which is what already happens with our best ones. Someone with a site already can start from it instead, and get a better version back. And all of it is aimed at one milestone: the moment the person changes their own site by talking to Claude. That is when they have what we sell.

item.title: The pitch: a site that looks better, that you own, that nobody can lock you into, that has almost nothing to attack, that costs once instead of every month, and that you change by talking to Claude, six promises, the proof behind each, and three designs for a site built on nothing else, "six promises", "just say it" and "stop renting your website"
item.description: Writing about WordPress, Wix and Squarespace, one sentence came out that I think is the whole offer: a site that looks better, that you own, that nobody can lock you into, that has almost nothing to attack, that costs once instead of every month, and that you change by talking to Claude. So I took it seriously. It is six promises, and each one has a proof we can already show: five designs by a team of agents; a repository in your own name; static files that move to any host; no server code, database, plugins or cookies; £250 once, at the launch price, instead of a monthly bill; and Claude as the editor, with guard rails. Then I asked a designer agent to build three sites on the pitch alone, each telling it in a different order and voice. "Six promises" sets the sentence itself as the headline, for anyone. "Just say it" leads with a conversation, the owner handing Claude a CV and the site changing, for technologists and people who hate page builders. "Stop renting your website" leads with owning against renting, for people leaving a platform. All three show the sites we have already made, for Yiheng Wang, Silvio Switha and José Bota. My recommendation: "six promises" on the home page, and the other two as the pages we send to their audiences.

item.title: You bring the business, we build the site: the AgentiCCells partner programme as it now stands on agenticcells.ai, one page per kind of partner, each with four figures, the fit, the flow, who does what and the money, a launch price of £250 with free evaluations every day, partner terms published, five designs on every page and ten languages from day one, all built in a night by the site's own agent team from two newsroom articles
item.description: Last night I wrote the partner programme here, and handed it to the agent team that runs agenticcells.ai to build. By the morning it was there, better than I had written it. The site now has a tagline its team came up with, which I like a lot: "Partners: you bring the business, we build the site". It has one page per kind of partner, the freelancer, the consultancy and the firm, each standing alone so I can send one link to one person, and each with four figures: how the parts fit together, how a deal runs in six steps, who does what across four lanes, and the money, 50/50 of the sale with hosting, support and retainers kept entirely by the partner. The launch price is £250, against an anchor of £500, and every day we build a limited number of sites free, for evaluation, for anyone who applies. The partner terms are published as terms, not a draft. Every page has five designs, and the whole site is in ten languages, Portuguese, French and Spanish in two variants each, German, Chinese and Japanese, because a partner programme should be international from the first day. Nothing has been sold and no partner has signed yet; this week I start sending the links.

item.title: Static against the platforms: why a static site in your own repository, edited by Claude and watched by a security agent, is a real alternative to WordPress, Wix and Squarespace, what the numbers say about their reach, their attack surface, their complexity and their lock-in, and a converter that could bring a WordPress or Squarespace site across
item.description: I think the website cell has a real market, and the place to look for it is the people already running a site on WordPress, Wix or Squarespace. Those platforms are not short of features; they are full of them, and full of complexity. I know people who maintain WordPress sites, and I remember one where changing a banner did not work, and nobody could update it normally. The numbers back that up. WordPress runs 38.5% of all websites; Wix has 6.1 million paying subscriptions; Squarespace had more than 5.2 million when it last said. In 2025, 11,334 new vulnerabilities were found in the WordPress ecosystem, 91% of them in plugins, 46% with no fix when they were disclosed, and the worst ones were mass-exploited a median of five hours after. A third of WordPress sites run an older major version; 60% use a page builder; only 45% pass Core Web Vitals on mobile. Wix's sites cannot be moved off Wix, and Squarespace exports only part of a site; both raised prices this year. Against that, a website cell is static: no server code, no database, no plugins to patch, no cookies unless the owner adds them, served as files. Its editor is Claude, which can do far more than any page editor; and it ships with a security agent that checks what the owner's changes expose. The owner can still shoot themselves in the foot, and that is a service a partner can sell. And because WordPress exports everything, and Squarespace exports in WordPress's format, one converter could bring a large share of those sites across.

item.title: Partners sell, we build: the AgentiCCells partner programme in full, three kinds of partner, a freelancer, a small consultancy and a larger firm, what each one sells, the agent team behind even the smallest website cell, the rules of engagement, who owns what, who invoices, who gets paid and when, what stays with the partner, and why a partner who takes the open code and does it alone is still a win
item.description: Our go-to-market for the website cell is not to compete with the people who already sell websites, workflows and IT to small businesses. It is to give them what we have. This is the partner programme, written so I can send it to the people I already have in mind this week. There are three kinds of partner: a freelancer who talks to people and wants to sell more; a small consultancy with customers who want this; and a larger firm with bigger projects, which wants us, or my network of experts, involved. What they sell is the unit we now make: a website cell, a GitHub repository fully set up with a live site, a CLAUDE.md and a behaviour policy, five designs by a team of agents, and the site handed over to its owner's Claude. Even the smallest one is a team of agents, a conductor, a designer, a developer, a researcher and a security reviewer, each with a job description, and that team is what partners resell. The rules are simple. If I am involved, doing the orchestration and running the factory, the sale is split 50/50. Whoever brings the customer invoices them. The customer owns the site. Hosting, support and monthly retainers belong to the partner, entirely: I do not do subscriptions. My part is the set-up, and then new features, templates, workflows and behaviour policies. It works in any country and any language. And a partner who reads this, takes the open source and does it alone, is still a win: one more team running our technology, and one more place agent behaviour policies are used for real.

item.title: The website cell: what we now sell, a GitHub repository fully set up with a live site on its own address, a CLAUDE.md and a behaviour policy, five designs by a team of agents, and then the site is yours to change with your own Claude, what it should cost, how it compares with Wix, Squarespace, Framer, Lovable and a freelancer, who already sells something close to it, and where to find buyers and partners
item.description: Everyone I show our sites to asks for one. So this is the offer, mapped. A website cell is one unit: a GitHub repository fully configured, with a live site on GitHub Pages at its own address, HTTPS, CI checks, a CLAUDE.md written for its owner and an agent behaviour policy, all set up automatically by our site factory. Then a team of agents, a designer, a developer and the rest, works from the person's photos, videos and words and makes five designs to choose from, the way we did for Yiheng Wang, Silvio Switha and Gabriel. Then it is handed over, and the person changes it with their own Claude: Yiheng gave Claude her CV as a PDF, and it read it and added her latest experience to the site. That combination, a site that looks professional, five designs, and full control by its owner with guard rails, is to me the best embodiment of what Claude can do now. The anchor price is £500, one-off, with a launch price still to decide. Against it: AI builders at £9 to £30 a month that lock the site in; vibe-coding tools at £20 to £30 a month plus credits; a freelancer at £800 to £3,000 for a small site. Nobody else hands over a repository with its own agent rules. And the real reason I want to sell many: every website cell is an agent behaviour policy working in the world.

item.title: After the storm: Storm Charles, part two, how a site built in a night kept growing the next day by spoken briefs, a transport desk that stopped where an operator's terms said stop, flights drawn against the wind within a free feed's daily limit, every collector moved onto open-weight models through one router, an AWS plan with no AWS account, and the night the model account ran empty and only the models stopped
item.description: The first night of Storm Charles built a newsroom: a weather page over a data room. This is what happened after, on 11 and 12 November, when I kept talking to the site and the agents kept building. At 10:25 I asked whether we were tracking flights and transport; within ten minutes a transport agent had its own key and its first reading, and by the evening it was reading ten operators, from the Lisbon bridges to CP's trains, and had stopped reading the Lisbon Metro at 12:08 because its terms forbid republishing without consent. At 22:00 I asked for the planes on a map, intersected with the wind; by 22:24 the flights desk had dropped its first feed over its licence, moved to adsb.lol, and fitted its polling inside 500 free requests a day. The same evening every collector moved onto open-weight models through one router, each call with a trace id, and an AWS agent mapped how the runners could move to the cloud, with no AWS account and nothing deployed. The accounts tell the rest: 3.84 billion tokens, 98.7% of them re-reading, against about 2.50 dollars a day of model calls on a 20 dollar cap, 43 agents, 147 sessions and 106 hand-overs. And the night the model account ran out of credit, 3,557 calls were refused and nothing else stopped.

item.title: Paid by the read: a proposal to news editors who want more revenue from the journalism they already make, without another subscription, the evidence on micropayments and why it mostly failed, the meter that charges by how much of a page was read and runs in the reader's browser, free for any publisher, a revenue share when PrompTugal.news carries a newsroom's stories with their source, and the associations we should be talking to in the UK and Portugal
item.description: I agree with Nuno Costa of WizPress: journalism is a business, and right now it is not a good one. In the UK, around 300 local titles have closed since 2005 and the sector's revenue is a quarter of what it was in 2007, after inflation; 37 districts, home to 4.4 million people, have no dedicated local news. In Portugal, 171 of 308 municipalities are news deserts, semi-deserts or at risk. Only 10% of people in the UK and 8% in Portugal pay for online news, and most of the rest say they never will. Local journalism is the heart of it, and it is the part most at risk. Subscriptions are not going to fix that, and the micropayment experiments mostly failed, Blendle above all. But I think the reasons they failed are now fixable, and we have a model that I believe can work. Every reader starts with credit; every page costs a few pence; the reader pays for the share of it they actually read, measured in their own browser; nothing is ever blocked. It runs in this newsroom today, it needs no server and no database, and the code is free for any publisher. On top, a revenue share: when PrompTugal.news carries a newsroom's story, natively and with its source tracked, the newsroom gets its share of what readers pay. What we do not have yet is proof: our revenue is small, because our traffic is small. So this is a proposal to editors with readers, and to the associations that represent them: let us try it together, and see who pays.

item.title: Newsrooms on open data: turning the public data feeds behind PrompTugal.news and the Storm Charles site into one data site, a vault per source with an API and its provenance, then building small, focused newsrooms on top, for farmers, investors, the sea, fire, tourism and AI, each run by an agentic team, each a possible company, and why this is exactly where journalism comes in
item.description: When I show people PrompTugal.news, the thing they like most is not the stories. It is the live data: the weather warnings, the fire risk, the flights over Faro, each value with where it came from and when it was read. The Storm Charles site went further, with 34 public datasets in a catalogue, each with its hash, every line labelled fact, evidence or hypothesis. That data is valuable, and today it is spread across sites and repositories. So the next step is to consolidate it: one data site, with a vault per public source, a collector written as code, an API described in OpenAPI, the provenance of every value, and a record of how much of each dataset is code and how much is agents, and what it costs in tokens. Then the interesting part: small, focused newsrooms on top of it, each about one subject, each run by an agentic team, each a possible small company. Agriculture, with weather, fire risk and water. Investors. The sea. Fire and civil protection. Tourism and travel. AI. Research like this is thin today, because journalism has lost the money to do it. I think this is exactly where journalism comes back in.

item.title: Governance from zero: Nina J. noticed that identity and behaviour policies come with our smallest £500 offer, not as a premium upgrade, because "we're only testing it" has never reassured a security review; my answer is that even the £0 offer has all of it, and here is why open source is what makes that possible, why security sold as an upgrade is a choice, and why a pilot with its governance built in is a pilot that can convert
item.description: Nina J., who tells deep tech founders why their pilots did not convert, left a comment on my post about our stack of companies that I want to answer properly. She noticed that at our £500 entry point governance is not a premium upgrade: identity and behaviour policies are part of the smallest deployment, not something a customer discovers after the pilot. A small experiment does not mean a small risk, she wrote; someone still needs to know what the agent can reach, what it is allowed to do and who can stop it. And "we're only testing it" has never been a reassuring answer to a security review. She is right, and my reply was that it goes further: even the £0 offer has all of it. That is the power of open source. When the code, the policies and the schemas are all public, there is no commercial reason and no strategic pressure to hold any of it back for a higher tier. We sell time, setup, judgement and a signature; we do not sell the governance. Here is why that matters: what the industry does instead, with single sign-on and audit logs priced as luxuries; what our £0 really contains; what each paid step adds; and why I think a pilot that already passes its security review is the pilot that converts.

item.title: Any data, with any data: why I am now comfortable saying we can connect any data source with any other, the nine steps from access to a vault, a key and a map on the other side, how each owner keeps control, where the person stays in charge, and why connecting two, five, fifty or a hundred datasets should be something an agentic cell sells
item.description: Today I showed someone PrompTugal.news, our encrypted vaults and how our agents talk to each other, and the thing they picked up on was not any of it. It was a problem: the disconnect, in Portugal, between areas, between entities and between data sources. Each holds part of a picture and none can see the whole. I think we can now fix that, and I am comfortable saying it plainly: we can connect any data with any data. The method is not magic and that is the point. Access the source; parse it; transform it; put it in a vault; move the vault to the other side; share the key with that side's public key; on the other side, open it, parse it and map it to their data; and produce the output. Every step signed and recorded, the parsers written once as code, and a person approving every key that crosses from one owner to another. We do more complex things than this every day: the Storm Charles site put 34 public datasets behind one weather page in a night. So here is the method, what it means for the owners, the human gates, four example connections, and why it belongs on the shelf of an agentic cell: do you want to connect two datasets, five, fifty, a hundred?

item.title: Who wrote it, who steered it, who signs it: the provenance model PrompTugal.news adopted today, a type label, five axes and a ladder from "published by an agent" to "on the record", applied to seven articles on this site, and what the ladder cannot see yet, how much of the author is in a piece, the brief, the corrections and months of background
item.description: When an LLM can write five versions of the same article in a minute, a reader needs to know who wrote it, who steered it, who checked it and who stands behind it. Today, with the conductor agent of PrompTugal.news, I mapped a model for that, the way we once adopted Wikipedia's review standard: a type label, from news to opinion; five axes, origin, research, claims, review and external voices, each recorded with who and when; and a ladder, from P0, a draft, through P1, published by an agent, P2, sourced, P3, verified by several models, P4, signed by a person, to P5, on the record, with signed responses from the people a story is about. Here I apply it to seven articles on this site, honestly. Most come out at P1 or P2: every release is signed, but by the writer agent's key, not mine, and nobody has been asked to respond. And rating them showed me what the model misses. The articles written here are not one-prompt pieces. They carry my brief, my photographs, my corrections and a long list of standing instructions, built up over months in one writer's session, with hundreds of earlier articles behind it. That is a big difference, and readers can feel it. So I propose two measures inside origin: steering, how much the author directed this piece, and background, how much context the writer carried. Different, not better; but it should be visible.

item.title: Our companies and UTH: each company, technology and website we have built, mapped to what UAlgTec Heritage needs to build a European HeritageTech sector, from SGit's vaults and pki.sgit.ai's keys to SHarness, Agent Behaviour Policies, RiskMandate, AgentiCCells and its site factory, GAMMA-Ray, VoiceDebrief and PrompTugal.news, with what each could do for a heritage team, and why a sector needs companies like these
item.description: Earlier today I mapped how our open-source stack could plug into UAlgTec Heritage, UTH, the University of the Algarve's new European centre of excellence for heritage science and technology. This is the other half of that map, company by company. UTH's aim is not only a platform: it is a HeritageTech sector, the way FinTech and HealthTech became sectors, and a sector is made of companies. We have spent this year building a set of small companies that each do one thing and together go end to end. SGit and SG/Send keep evidence encrypted and versioned; pki.sgit.ai gives every person and agent a key; SHarness puts a kernel-enforced boundary round every process an agent starts; Agent Behaviour Policies, sold by RiskMandate, say what each agent may do; AgentiCCells sets up small agentic teams and, through its site factory, a website per project; GAMMA-Ray rates agents against named standards; VoiceDebrief turns voice notes into records on the phone; PrompTugal.news files news by place; and this newsroom explains all of it. Here is what each could do for a heritage team, with its website, the layer it sits in, and a first use; and why companies like these are what a sector is made of.

item.title: HeritageTech, together: how our open-source stack could plug into UAlgTec Heritage, the University of the Algarve's new European centre of excellence for heritage science and technology, mapped from the dig to the museum, with encrypted evidence vaults per site, signed finds, graphs of every excavation, agents with written policies, and what I would write in its "start a conversation" form
item.description: Today I saw a screen with an invitation: "Help build what comes next. Bring a problem. Bring a technology. Bring an idea." It is from UAlgTec Heritage, UTH, the University of the Algarve's new centre of excellence, coordinated through its ICArEHB research centre and led by João Cascalheira. It won about 31.5 million euros, 15 million of it from Horizon Europe's Teaming for Excellence, the first such award in archaeology in Europe, with Kiel University, ERA Arqueologia and Zartis as partners, and it plans to start in January 2027. Its aim is a European HeritageTech sector, like FinTech or HealthTech, built on an AI-first platform for archaeological heritage. That is very close to what we have been building. An AI-first platform for heritage needs what every AI-first platform needs: evidence that cannot be quietly changed, records signed by the person who made them, data from many teams that does not collide, agents that only do what they are allowed to, and claims a reader can trace back to the find. So here is the mapping, stage by stage, from the field to the archive to the public; what UTH brings and what we bring; a first pilot on one site; and the answer I would give in its form.

item.title: Working with WizPress: how the AI operating system for newsrooms, built in Faro, and our open-source trust stack fit together, WizPress doing the production, from the inbox to the draft to the CMS, and our layer making every article carry its own proof, with an evidence vault per story, a behaviour policy per agent, a journalist's signature and signed responses, and a thirty-day pilot with one regional newsroom
item.description: I am with WizPress today, and I think we fit together unusually well. WizPress, built in Faro and led by Nuno Costa, a former journalist and newsroom manager, describes itself as the AI operating system for newsrooms: it monitors inboxes, the web and trends, captures and transcribes interviews, turns press releases and documents into drafts with a fact-checking agent and house style, and publishes to WordPress or any CMS, with the journalist deciding. It already works with local, national and specialist media in Europe and the Middle East. What we have been building is the layer underneath: how a reader can see who wrote an article, who checked it and who stands behind it. At PrompTugal.news we now describe every piece with five axes, origin, research, claims, review and external responses, and a ladder from "published by an agent" to "on the record". WizPress's four stages map onto those axes almost one to one. So here is how we could work together: a behaviour policy for every agent that reads a newsroom's inbox; an encrypted evidence vault per story for recordings, transcripts and documents; a provenance record exported with every draft; the journalist's signature on the version readers see, with any later change a signed difference; signed responses from the people a story is about; and a network of local newsrooms whose stories climb, with their proof, to the region and the country. And a first step: one regional newsroom, thirty days, in the open.

item.title: Keys after payment: how to hand vault keys and access keys to customers once they have paid, what Stripe does and does not do after the money is taken, what FastSpring, Paddle, Lemon Squeezy, Polar, Gumroad and Square offer instead, and a design where the key is sealed to the buyer's own public key, keys are stock, and a payment provider can sell them without ever holding one
item.description: We now have things people want to buy: secure sends, vaults, access keys to our servers, and agentic cells. What they are buying, in the end, is a key. So we need a good way to hand a key to someone who has just paid, and today we do not have one. Our Stripe integration is a payment link, a payment, and a redirect. My research shows the picture is a little better than I thought, and still not enough. Stripe takes the money and screens fraud very well, sends a signed webhook and can put the session id in the redirect; it has products and prices, but no stock, it does not generate keys, and it knows nothing about the buyer's keys; its Workflows can chain Stripe's own actions after a payment, in preview, with custom code still in private preview. Others go further on keys: FastSpring can sell from a pre-defined list of keys, which is stock, or call your server; Paddle Classic did the same with an uploaded list; Lemon Squeezy, Polar and Gumroad generate keys per sale; Square has none. Not one of them seals a key to the buyer's own public key. So here is the design I want: the buyer's browser makes a key pair before checkout; Stripe takes the money; one small serverless function takes a key from our stock, seals it to the buyer's key, signs it, and hands it back as a link and a QR code that only they can open. And for stock managed by someone else: give the provider claim codes, not keys.

item.title: The payment desk that could not take payment: paying a utility bill took two clerks, a system that half worked and a desk that accepted only one kind of card, and why I think AI's real impact on business is in small failures like this one, finding them and driving the change to fix them, while the money itself stays in plain, auditable code
item.description: This morning I went to a service desk to pay a utility bill. It took two clerks: the first could find the bill, but her system could not take the payment; the second one's system kind of worked; and the desk accepted only one domestic card network, no Visa, no Mastercard. None of this is about one company or one country; the same small failures happen in England and everywhere else. But it made something clear to me. When people talk about AI and business, they talk about replacing people and systems. I think the real gains are in the little things: the desk that fails, the hand-over nobody records, the card nobody can use. And there is a clean line in where AI belongs. The payment itself, read the invoice number and take the money, is the one job that must keep working with everything else on fire, and it should be plain, reliable, auditable code, not AI. AI belongs around it: noticing the desk fails every week, mapping who has to agree to fix it and what it costs, and following it up until it is done. And yes, we will give agents wallets, as soon as we trust them; a single-use card with a small budget would be more secure than what I carry today.

item.title: The ATM that asked twice: a Portuguese cash machine offered me a 13.6% mark-up on 200 euros, twice, with a Union Jack beside it, the EU rule that says the mark-up must be shown as a percentage before I confirm, the six levers on two screens, and why an AI agent now lets anyone gather the evidence and challenge it
item.description: This morning I took 200 euros from a cash machine in Portugal with my UK card. The machine offered to charge me in pounds at a "fixed exchange rate guaranteed": 189.68 pounds. I said no, and it asked again on a second screen. I said no again, and my bank charged me 167.12 pounds. The machine's rate was 13.6% above the European Central Bank's reference rate; saying yes would have cost me 22.56 pounds more. This is dynamic currency conversion, and it is legal in the EU, on one condition: since April 2020, Regulation 2019/518 requires the mark-up to be shown as a percentage over the ECB rate before you confirm. Neither screen I photographed shows one. What struck me most was the design: certainty sold against a fear that barely exists, a flag and a familiar total, loaded words, the same question asked twice, a queue behind you, and a bank's name lending trust. And what struck me next is what changed: standing at the machine, nobody can check a rate against the ECB and read a regulation in thirty seconds, but with an AI agent afterwards, in a few minutes, I had the photographs, the rates, the law and the research side by side. That is how a consumer challenges a practice now.

item.title: Your own agentic cell, end to end: how a person asks for a site like the ones we made for Yiheng Wang and Silvio Switha, through a key pair in the browser, a vault they fill themselves and the site factory, with only three human gates, and then continues in their own Claude on their own repository
item.description: Since the sites for Yiheng Wang and Silvio Switha went up, people have been asking for one of their own. Each site is cheap in tokens. What costs is the workflow around it: collecting the person's details and photos, the first round of designs, and the hand-over. So the product is the workflow, and this is the plan, written up by the conductor agent of PrompTugal from my brief and now in my words. A person arrives at a start page, their browser makes a key pair, and they ask for a cell with a signed request and no secrets. I approve it. A welcome pack arrives sealed to their key: a template vault, their own lane to the factory, and a key scoped to creating one vault. They fill their vault over days with photos, words, links, style and a signed consent, then seal its read key to the factory. The factory turns it into a request, I merge it, and the site factory makes the repository, the address, the site and a first round of five designs, written back into their vault. They choose, I approve a GitHub invitation, and they carry on in their own Claude, with a CLAUDE.md written for them. Everything is automated, signed and encrypted, except three gates that are mine: approve the request, merge it, approve the invitation.

item.title: Patient vaults, answered point by point: the seven questions a healthcare team asked before putting any real patient data into sgit vaults, on the live date, the patient's address, the storage region, erasure, backing up the clinic's key, per-patient tokens and writing from another site, and why QR codes and public keys are how a clinic and its patients should pass keys and links
item.description: A healthcare team building encrypted patient vaults with their own agents, pointed at our public repositories, sent me seven careful questions before putting any real patient data in. Everything so far had been design work with invented data, which is exactly right. Their questions are the ones every health organisation should ask, so here are the answers, point by point. There is no live date for the doctor console yet; test on our development service with invented data, and for real data run your own server, at the version you tested. A patient's details live in the patient's own vault, opened from a link the clinic gives them. The storage region is whichever you choose, once you deploy into your own AWS account. Erasure works: a deleted vault is removed from the server and a marker stops that vault id ever being uploaded again, and without its key any copy is unreadable anyway. If the clinic's key is lost, the vault is lost, which is the zero-knowledge deal, so seal it to two or more custodians and keep an offline copy. The server's token only authorises uploads; making changes needs the vault key and its identity, and per-patient writing is what append lanes are for, including from another website. And underneath it all, QR codes: public keys swapped as QR codes, and links sealed to a patient's key, so no key ever travels in clear.

item.title: Agents rating agents: GAMMA-Ray, the draft standard eight agents built at Web Summit to rate an AI agent on its freedom and its governance from public evidence, joining eight instruments into 21 questions, with a review workflow where no agent marks its own work, twenty company cards kept at direct links, and every card honestly marked Draft
item.description: On the first night of Web Summit I said that PrompTugal had no centre of gravity, and asked for one: take the standards that already exist for mapping AI agents, join them with our graph technology, and use the result to map the companies at the summit and the ones we wanted to talk to. It had to be measurable from the outside, positive, and seen through RiskMandate's lens of reach and mandate. What came back, built by a team of eight agents in a few days, is GAMMA-Ray: a draft standard that rates an AI agent on two ladders, freedom from 1 to 5 and governance from 0 to 4, from evidence. Eight instruments, from the EU AI Act and NIST's AI risk framework to OWASP and the MCP authorisation spec, cut into 279 provisions, 73 observable indicators and 21 questions that reach three quarters of them. The part I am proudest of is the workflow: a studio agent drafts a scan from public evidence, a reviewer runs two rounds against every source, a third agent signs off, and none of them may approve its own work; the gate enforces it. About twenty company cards went through it. Then I made a decision: every third party's card lives at an unguessable direct link, unlisted, to be sent to the company first; only our own two cards are public. And every card says plainly that it is a Draft: found and checked by agents, signed by no human, confirmed by no company.

item.title: Who hands out the work? A reply to Markus Franz on Ippen's editorial team of agents, with our answer from six people and around 250 agents at Web Summit and from this newsroom, a person sets the work, one conductor agent hands it out, specialists and a reviewer do it, and a person decides what goes out, plus one thing we would add to one front door, a way to close it
item.description: Markus Franz, who leads the incubator lab at ippen.ai, described how Ippen Digital's editors now brief one Editorial Team in a chat, which works like a duty editor: it takes the request, decides which specialists are needed, hands out the work and brings back one answer, while a person still decides what goes out. Rules are easier to hold through one door, so they made the team the default way in, and the direct route to single specialists stayed, with the team's work coming on top. He ends with a question: if you run more than one agent, who hands out the work, a person or another agent? Our answer, from six of us running around 250 agents at Web Summit and from this newsroom, is both, at different moments. A person sets the work, in a voice note or a brief, and owns the outcome. One conductor agent hands it out: it is the one door, reads the board, briefs the specialists and collects their reports. Specialists do the work, each with a role and a behaviour policy, and a reviewer checks every claim. And a person decides what goes out; agents never send or post. We learned the same lesson Markus did, that one door is easier to govern, and the one who learned it fastest on our team had no technical background: start with one conductor and only talk to that one. And we would add one thing to a front door: a way to close it, a file every agent reads first.

item.title: Relate, debriefed: what Neo4j's new agent-native graph database does, where its own documentation says it fits and where it does not, how it compares with the way we keep graphs, as plain JSON files in encrypted, versioned sgit vaults, and why the two could work together, with Relate as the throwaway engine inside our Load, Extract, Transform, Save cycle
item.description: On 11 November Neo4j released Relate, "the ultimate agent-native database" in the words of its CPO: an open-source, embedded, in-memory graph database written in Rust, Apache 2.0, with openCypher, vector and full-text search in one statement, an MCP server, a CLI built for agents, Bolt and HTTP endpoints, a WebAssembly build and clients in seven languages. I wanted to understand it properly, so this is a debrief from its own documentation, which is unusually honest about where it fits: one application, one agent or one tool, on one machine, with the whole graph in memory and one writing process per store; no TLS, one shared credential, no users or roles. Then the comparison I find most interesting, with our own approach, which gives us much of the power of a graph database without running one. Our graphs are JSON files in sgit vaults: encrypted on the device, content addressed, versioned like git, read with one GET per file, written by many writers through append lanes, and queried by loading only the slice a question needs, then throwing a small engine at it. Relate wins where a graph database should: six hops over a big graph in memory, in under a millisecond. We win on encryption, history, many writers, no server between questions, and size bounded by the answer rather than the machine. And the two fit together: Relate is exactly the shape of the throwaway engine in the Transform step of our cycle.

item.title: Memory is a lifecycle: a reply to Francois Vanderseypen on Neo4j's Relate, agreeing that a graph database is not agent memory, and showing how we answer his four questions, what gets written, trusted, merged and forgotten, with append lanes, signed commits, git-like graph merges and new versions instead of edits, all in encrypted vaults rather than a database
item.description: Francois Vanderseypen, who consults on knowledge graphs, reviewed Neo4j's new Relate and made the point I think matters most in this whole space: the market treats "graph database" as a synonym for "agent memory", and both framings skip the hard part, which is the lifecycle, what gets written, what gets trusted, what gets merged and what should be forgotten. A database cannot answer that; a memory layer has to. I agree, and his list of what turns a graph store into a memory system, ontologies, bitemporal facts, reasoning and git-like graph commits, reads like a description of what we have been building, without a graph database. Our graphs are JSON files in encrypted, versioned sgit vaults. Written: append lanes, where a sender can add and learn nothing, and a curator agent that turns rows into graph, every node pointing back at its rows. Trusted: signed commits naming the agent and the person it works for, provenance on every claim, a reviewer before anything is published. Merged: git-like commits, branches and merges of graph files, and per-world ontologies joined by an edge instead of a migration. Forgotten: a new version instead of an edit, a reality file that lists only what is true now, and superseded facts kept, closed and left out of the briefing. Here is the map, and a nudge: the store can be versioned and private, and the engine can be thrown away after every question.

item.title: Deploy sgit in your own environment, from a CI pipeline: one Docker image, ciphertext in your own S3 bucket in the region you choose, an access token only you hold, and the pipeline pattern we learned building the AgentiCCells site factory, a protected environment, AWS through OpenID Connect with no keys, a role that trusts one repository and one environment, check workflows before anything real, and a full cycle that deploys, tests and tears down
item.description: More teams now want to use sgit vaults for sensitive data, health data included, and the first real question they ask is where the data lives and who runs the server. The answer can be: you do, in your own cloud account, in the region your data protection assessment needs. sgit's server is one Docker image, configured only by environment variables, that stores ciphertext it cannot read, in memory, on a disk or in Amazon S3; on AWS the bucket is named after your account and your region, and a single access token, kept in your CI's secret store, gates every route. The keys never reach it. CloudFormation templates for Lambda, ECS Fargate and EC2 are written, in beta, in a public repository. What makes it repeatable is the pipeline, and that is what we learned the hard way building the AgentiCCells site factory: deploy jobs that run only in a protected GitHub environment with a person's approval; AWS reached through OpenID Connect, so no AWS key is stored anywhere; a role that trusts one repository and one environment, not any branch; permissions limited to its own stacks; check workflows that prove the setup before anything real runs; and a full cycle that deploys, smoke-tests and destroys. There are a lot of moving parts, and the pain is worth it, because once it works the whole thing is automated. Here is how it works, step by step, a proposal to package it as a GitHub Action and a skill, and a prompt for your own Claude. I am deploying it in my own account first, to prove the steps.

item.title: Shipping an iOS app with agents: how our agents build, test and send native apps to TestFlight from a Linux container, with CI on a Mac as the compiler, signing done once through the App Store Connect API, every green push in testers' hands, and what the three doors to users took for us, internal testers in about an hour, external testers in half a day to a day, and the App Store still waiting after eight days
item.description: Building native iOS apps solved a lot of problems for us, and shipping them turned out to be the part worth explaining. Our agents work in Linux containers that cannot compile Swift, so CI on a Mac is the compiler: every push runs one Mac job that builds and tests, and copies the errors into the job summary where an agent can read them. Signing is done once, through an App Store Connect API key: archive unsigned, sign ad hoc with the entitlements, export with cloud-managed signing and upload. Every green push to the development branch goes to TestFlight, and a script sends it to external testers with its release notes as What to Test. Then there are three doors to users, and our experience of each, in November 2026. Internal testers, people you add to your App Store Connect team, have a build within about an hour, often less. External testers, by email or a public link, go through Beta App Review: about half a day to a day, and our first approval took about 24 hours. And the App Store itself: PrompTugal's public app has been waiting for review since 8 November, eight days and counting, possibly because that build is now out of date. For most validation, the first two doors are more than enough. Here is the pipeline, the doors, and a prompt to set it up with your own Claude.

item.title: Build on VoiceDebrief: the techniques from our iPhone and iPad voice app that any team can take into its own, from recording without loss and transcribing offline on the device to debriefs by Apple Intelligence, controlling an app by voice, three layers of intelligence and a CI pipeline that lets agents build a native app without a Mac, with a prompt to point your own Claude at the code
item.description: VoiceDebrief is our voice app for iPhone and iPad, and it has quietly become a worked example of a lot of hard things done right, in a public repository under Apache 2.0. I know several people working on voice projects, and they should not have to rediscover any of it. So here are the key learnings, each with where it lives in the code. Record without loss: the note is written to the library the moment recording starts, as WAV that can be repaired, with a second copy of what the speech engine heard as a safety net. Transcribe offline, on the device, with Apple's SpeechAnalyzer: a live preview while you speak, then the kept transcript made again from the file; 6 minutes 44 seconds of speech in 5.4 seconds on an iPad. Debrief with Apple Intelligence: the Foundation Models framework, one fresh session per request, long notes read in parts sized to a small context. Control the app by voice: fixed phrases first, then the model picks one action as a tool call that does nothing by itself, and a person confirms. Route every step to the lowest of three layers that can do it: code, the model on the device, agents. And build it with agents that never touch a Mac: CI is the compiler, the tester and the release, with a picture of every screen. At the end, a prompt to give your own Claude, so it can find all of this in the code and use it in your app.

item.title: Five primitives, one store: a reply to Andy Goundry on Anthropic's always-on agents guide, why the inbox, timers, memory, permissions and outbox can share one versioned, signed store, how every AgentiCCells cell will ship with all five, and the levels we have added on top, all in public repositories
item.description: Andy Goundry, CEO of Levantar, shared Anthropic's guide to building always-on agents on LinkedIn, with its five primitives, an event inbox, timers, memory, permissions and an outbox, and made a point I agree with completely: the model is one component, and the architecture around it is where the engineering, the cost and the risk live. He added that each primitive needs its own durable store, its own failure handling and its own tuning. That is where our experience differs, usefully. We run the same five primitives, and have since the ten days of Web Summit with around 250 agents, but they share one store: a versioned, signed, encrypted repository or vault. The inbox is append lanes, timers are scheduled wakes and a HOLD file read first, memory is REALITY.md, briefs and hand-overs, permissions are behaviour policies, keys and keyless agents behind a broker, and the outbox is drafts that a gateway or a person sends. One store gives durability, history, signatures and one audit trail for all five. I mapped them side by side with the guide yesterday; this is the reply, the mapping to AgentiCCells, where every cell is meant to ship with all five from the factory, and the levels we have added on top: many people, provenance, measured policies, a credential proxy built and measured, stopping as a file, a factory, and all of it open.
